cards.text: Paul is writing a letter to God's people in Rome. He just finished telling them to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21). Now he turns to the governing authorities, the people in charge.

cards.question: Paul says only the believers in Rome must submit to the governing authorities.
Why does Paul say everyone must submit to the governing authorities?

answers.text: There is no authority except from God
Rulers always know what is best
The law of Moses commands it

cards.text: Paul says, "The authorities that exist have been appointed by God." So whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and friend, I argued with an oven timer ONCE and lost.

cards.question: Paul says whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and will bring ___ on themselves.

cards.text: Next, Paul talks about rulers, and who ought to be nervous around them. A police car pulls up behind me in traffic and I start SWEATING, and I'm a cookie stamper who doesn't even drive.

cards.question: Paul says rulers are a terror to good conduct.
Paul asks if you want to be unafraid of the one in authority. His answer is to do what is right.

cards.text: Do what is right, Paul says, and "you will have his approval."

cards.question: Paul says the one in authority is God's ___ for your good.

cards.text: But then Paul flips it. If you do wrong, he says, be afraid.

cards.question: If you do wrong, Paul says to be afraid of the one in authority, because he does not carry the ___ in vain.

cards.text: Paul says, "He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer." Then Paul gets to his "therefore."

cards.question: Paul says it's necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment. What's the other reason?
Paul says the same reasons for submitting to authority are also why you pay something. What is it?

cards.text: Paul says the authorities are God's servants, who devote themselves to their work. Years in a junk drawer, the tax man never found me, and friend, nobody else did EITHER.

cards.question: Paul says to pay everyone what you owe. Besides taxes and revenue, he lists two things you owe in how you treat people: ___ and ___.

cards.text: Paul's whole list: "taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due." That's a long bill, friend, and half of it you can't pay with money.

findings.problem: The card says Paul is writing to God's people in Rome. This fact comes from outside the passage, and the card gives no reference for it (Romans 1:1, 1:7). Only Romans 12:21 is cited.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The joke has Papa Dorin sitting in traffic with a police car behind him. That adds something new to his world. He lives alone on a cookie planet just big enough for his bakery, and his past is the Millers' kitchen and the junk drawer. It is not a small moment around his bakery.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The card only repeats what card 8 just established, that doing right earns the ruler's approval. It adds nothing new and has none of Papa Dorin's voice.
The card is stripped down to a bare paraphrase with no Papa Dorin voice. Cards 9, 11 and 13 come close together and are all flat, so this stretch of the walkthrough reads without his humor.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The fact on this card is that the authorities devote themselves to their work. The joke is about the tax man never finding him in the drawer. That is a different action, so the comparison doesn't match the fact. It also reads like dodging taxes, right after Paul says to pay them.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The question asks for two things you owe "in how you treat people." The wrong answers (gifts, tithes, offerings) are things you hand over, not ways of treating people. The question wording rules them out, so the baker can answer without knowing the verse.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The two right answers are assigned to fixed blanks: respect to blank 1 and honor to blank 2. Nothing in the question sets the order. A baker who puts honor in blank 1 and respect in blank 2 has the meaning right but would be marked wrong.
findings.question: When a two-blank card has two right answers that could go in either order, should the question be worded so the order is clear, should either order count as right, or should cards like this be avoided?
